chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ibrahim ibn Muhammad, who said: Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Khorasani wrote:

A man bequeathed to me, and he left only sons of the paternal uncle, daughters of the paternal uncle, a paternal uncle, and two paternal aunts. To whom does the inheritance belong? He wrote to him with peace: 'The people of the 'asabah (residuary heirs) and the sons of the paternal uncle are the heirs.'
Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: This report is consistent with the Sunni view, but we do not adopt it; rather, we adopt what preceded from the reports.

key_terms.أَهْلُ الْعَصَبَةِ: People of the residuary heirs (those who inherit the remainder)
key_terms.لِلْعَامَّةِ: With the general public (referring to Sunni jurists)

ai.seo_question: How do Shia jurists view the inheritance rights of paternal uncles compared to Sunni jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration highlights a key jurisprudential divergence in Shia inheritance law regarding the 'asabah (residuary heirs) when closer kin are absent. While the report aligns with the Sunni view that paternal uncles and their descendants inherit, Shaykh al-Tusi notes that Muhammad ibn al-Hasan rejects this specific ruling in favor of earlier Shia traditions, emphasizing the school's distinct methodological independence from the general jurists (al-ammah).
